title: Two: An Inventory of Small Things

blocks.c: Two: An Inventory of Small Things
May was the month of the houses, and the houses nearly finished her.

There is a way of doing this work that is taught, and Ilse had taught it herself to four trainees, and it goes as follows. You do not begin by looking. Looking is the enemy. If you walk into a room and look at it you will see the interesting things, and you will record the interesting things, and thirty years later somebody will want to know what the ordinary things were and you will have failed them.

So you begin at the door and you go clockwise. You record every wall, every fitting, every object, in the order it comes, whether or not it is worth recording, and you photograph each wall from the opposite corner, and you write the number of the exposure in the notebook beside the entry, and you do not skip a shelf because it is only jam jars. Especially not because it is only jam jars.
Ilse did thirty-one houses in five weeks that way, alone, from half past seven in the morning until the light went.
She found, among other things:

items: A complete set of harness for a heavy horse, hanging in a stable, oiled within the last two years, in a village where the last working horse had gone in 1958.
Forty-one folding chairs in the village hall, of which thirty-nine were the same pattern and two were not, and the two had been repaired with brass plates by somebody who cared.

A cupboard under a stair containing nine hundred glass photographic negatives, quarter plate, unlabelled, which turned out to be the life's work of a Mr. Aled Stammers, blacksmith and photographer, between about 1898 and 1931, and which she got out of the valley in eleven boxes and which are now the most consulted collection in the county.
In the shop, behind the counter, a ledger of credit given, running from 1936 to 1971, with running balances for every household in the village, never once totalled, never once chased.
A mousetrap in the parish chest, empty, and a mousetrap in the school, occupied.

blocks.c: She got into a rhythm and the rhythm carried her, and by the end of the third week she had stopped noticing that she was living alone in a condemned valley and had started to be irritated when anybody interrupted her.
Cordell interrupted her on the twelfth of May.
The programme
"They've brought the grave licence forward," he said. "July the second. I'm sorry. It was August."
Ilse put down the tape measure. They were in the chapel, which was Baptist, and severe, and had been closed since 1969, and which she had been recording for two hours in the cold.
"Why?"

"Because the contractor who does exhumations is a specialist and there are four of them in the country and one of them has gone bankrupt, so everybody's programme has moved." He said it heavily. "It's eleven weeks of work. Two hundred and six stones, and every one has to be lifted, recorded, moved and re-erected at Culverton, and everything under them has to be taken up and reinterred, and there is a licence and a procedure and a diocesan man who comes and stands there."
"I'll need to have finished the churchyard survey before they start."
"You'll need to have finished it by the twenty-eighth of June."

Ilse looked at her list. She had the church, the chapel, the school, the mill, the hall, the smithy, the pumping engine, eleven barns, and two hundred and six gravestones, and it was the twelfth of May.
"Then I will finish it by the twenty-eighth of June," she said.
"Miss Vanterpool—"

"Mr. Cordell, when I was twenty-four I catalogued the papers of an estate office that had burned in a fire, wet, in a barn, in February, in six weeks, and this is a churchyard in June." She picked the tape measure up again. "I would like one thing, though, and it is not an assistant."
"Ask."
"The Board's photographs of the valley. The survey ones, from before the scheme. Aerial, if there are any."
"There are. Nineteen-sixty-six, for the reservoir design. Why?"

"Because I have a churchyard plan on linen that shows plots and a churchyard on the ground that shows stones, and the two do not entirely agree," said Ilse, "and I would like a third thing that agrees with neither, so I can find out which of them is lying."
The school

The school at Hallowmere closed in 1963, when the roll fell to nine, and the building had been used since as a store for the village hall, which meant that everything in it was still in it, under thirty years of other things.
She began on it on the fifteenth of May and it took eleven days and it changed the shape of the whole commission.

A village school of that period keeps four kinds of record and Hallowmere had all four. There was an admission register, which lists every child admitted, with date of birth, name of parent, previous school and date of leaving. There was an attendance register, weekly, in printed columns. There was a punishment book, which she read with a sort of dismal fascination and which recorded, over sixty years, a remarkably consistent local view about what a boy might reasonably be hit for. And there was a log book.

The log book is the thing. Every school kept one, by law, and the head teacher was required to enter in it the events of the school's life — closures, epidemics, visits by inspectors, notable weather — and to enter nothing else. What that produces, over ninety years, is the single best account of a village that exists anywhere, written by the one person in it whose job was to be exact.
Hallowmere's log book runs from 1875 to 1963 in three volumes, and the second volume covers the war.
Ilse read it in the caravan over four evenings.
3 September 1940. School reopened after summer. Roll 38.

14 September 1940. Notification received from the county that this school will receive evacuated children from Ferrisport, with their teacher, Miss A. Prosser. Accommodation to be found. Roll from Monday 79.
16 September 1940. Forty-one children arrived by bus at 2 p.m. with Miss Prosser. All were billeted by 6 p.m. except two, who slept at the schoolhouse. Roll 79.
17 September 1940. Two shifts instituted, Hallowmere children in the morning, Ferrisport children in the afternoon, on the advice of the county. This is not satisfactory and I shall say so.
Forty-one children arrived.
Ilse went back to the admission register and counted the Ferrisport admissions of September 1940, and there were thirty-nine.

She counted them again in the morning, when she was fresh, and there were thirty-nine, and she wrote them out in a list with their dates of birth and their parents' names and the Ferrisport school they had come from, and thirty-nine is what there were.

Then she went through the attendance register for the autumn term of 1940 and counted the names in the Ferrisport columns, and there were forty-one, and the two extra were N. Braith and T. Braith, and they appear in the attendance register every week from the twentieth of September 1940, and they never appear in the admission register at all.
She sat back.

An admission register is the formal document; it goes to the county and it is what a school is funded on. An attendance register is the working document; it is filled in twice a day by a teacher who has thirty-nine or forty-one children in front of her and no time to be political about it.
The two extra children were in the room. They were simply not on the paper that mattered.
Miss Prosser

She read the log book to the end of the war that night with the paraffin heater ticking and the valley black outside, and afterwards she could not have said whether what she felt was excitement or shame, because both of them feel identical at one in the morning.

2 October 1940. Miss Prosser has asked whether two of her children may be entered on the attendance register only, their papers having been lost in the raid of 26 August. I have entered them. The county may make of it what it wishes.

11 November 1940. Miss Prosser has been three times to the billeting officer about the Braith children and has come back three times with nothing. She is a formidable woman and I would not care to be the billeting officer.
19 December 1940. Christmas concert. The Ferrisport children sang. Mrs. Ammons at the piano. Nell Braith spoke a piece and was very good.
And then, more than a year later, in a different ink and a noticeably worse hand:
12 February 1942. School closed by order of the Medical Officer of Health, diphtheria having been confirmed in the village. Six cases. I have sent the children home with instructions.
23 February 1942. School reopened. Roll 71. We have lost five.
24 February 1942. Nothing to record.
25 February 1942. Nothing to record.
26 February 1942. Nothing to record.
Four words, three times, in a book whose entire purpose was to record.

Ilse had read enough log books to know that a head teacher writes nothing to record about a week in which nothing happens, and does not write it about the week after five of her children have been buried, and that these three entries were the sound of a woman sitting at a desk with a pen and being unable to do her job.
She wrote in her notebook:

Log book, 12-26 Feb 1942. Five deaths confirmed from the school's side. Consistent with register. Note however: log book says six cases and five deaths, which is an extraordinary case fatality rate for diphtheria in 1942, when antitoxin was available and the MOH would have been on it within a day. Check MOH annual report, county archive. Check newspapers. Check death certificates at the registrar's — five certificates should exist.
Note also: the two Braith children appear on the attendance register from Sept 1940 and never on the admission register. Their papers were said to be lost. They are two of the five who died.
She underlined the last sentence twice, which she never did, and then in the morning she was embarrassed by the underlining and did not cross it out, because crossing out is falsification.
Her mother's box
The box came on the twenty-first of May, sent up from her flat by her neighbour at her own request, and she had put off asking for it for a month.

When her mother died there had been very little. A nursing home room reduces a life to what fits on two shelves. There was a wedding photograph, and a wristwatch, and a Bible she had never once seen her mother open, and a biscuit tin of documents, and four cardigans that Ilse had given to the home.

She had gone through the tin in January, sitting on the floor of her flat, in the flat competent way she did everything, and had found: a marriage certificate; a birth certificate for Ilse; a rent book from 1954; three ration books; a photograph of a woman in a WVS uniform who Ilse had never identified; and her mother's own birth certificate, which recorded the birth of Marta Rhys, on the ninth of March, 1931, at Ferrisport, to Elin Rhys, no father named.
She had looked at that in January and had thought: so she was illegitimate, and never said, and that explains a good deal.
She looked at it again in May, in a caravan behind a village hall in a valley that was going to be flooded, and she thought something entirely different.
Marta Rhys. Aged eleven in February 1942.
No. 411. Rhys, Marta. Age 11. Abode: Hallowmere. Buried 14 February 1942.

The birth certificate in her hand was a certified copy, not an original. It had been issued — the stamp said so — in October 1949, from the register office at Ferrisport, which had been bombed in 1940, and whose records had been reconstituted after the war from whatever could be found.

Ilse sat in the caravan for a long time with a paraffin heater ticking and a piece of paper in her hand and did what she had been trained to do, which is to say she wrote down exactly what she had, and exactly what it did and did not prove.
Certified copy of an entry of birth, issued Ferrisport 1949, for Marta Rhys, b. 9 March 1931, mother Elin Rhys.
Burial register Hallowmere records burial of Marta Rhys, aged 11, of Hallowmere, 14 February 1942. If b. March 1931, she would have been 10 at the date of burial, not 11.
These may be two different people. Rhys is a common name.
These may be the same person, in which case one of the two documents is false.
There is no version of this in which both documents are true.
She read that over twice.
Then she wrote, underneath, in a hand that was not as steady as she would have liked:
If the burial entry is false, someone in this valley wrote a false entry in a parish register in 1942 and my mother is the reason.
What she did next
What she did next was nothing, for eleven days, which is the part she was later least able to explain to anybody.

She worked. She finished the school and started the mill. She catalogued the pumping engine, and got a specialist down from the museum to look at it, and had the satisfaction of watching a man of sixty stand in a shed and say a swear word very quietly. She did four barns.

She did not go to the county archive to look at the Medical Officer's report. She did not write to the registrar for the death certificates. She did not go and see Emrys Pike, whose name was on a stone under the yew, and who was eleven days older than the dead boy would have been.
She thought about it constantly and she did none of it, and towards the end of that fortnight she came to understand why, and it was not pleasant.
She was afraid that it was true.

Not afraid of the truth in the abstract; she had spent her professional life saying, at meetings, in a level voice, that the record is the record. She was afraid, specifically, of the version of the story in which her mother's silence had been a lie rather than a wound. She had spent thirty-nine years believing that her mother did not talk about the war because the war had been terrible. If this was true, her mother had not talked about the war because her mother had been someone else, and had decided, at some point, to be Marta Rhys, and had gone on deciding it every day for forty years, including all the days when she had been sitting across a kitchen table from her own daughter.
That is not a wound. That is a policy.
On the second of June she woke up at four in the morning with the answer, and it was so simple that she laughed out loud in the dark.

She did not have to decide anything. She was not there as a daughter. She was there as an archivist with a statutory commission and eleven weeks to go, and there was a churchyard to survey, and a churchyard survey records every stone in the ground and what is cut on it, and the two nameless stones under the yew were part of her commission, and so was the plan, and so was the burial fee book she had not yet opened.
She could do her job. Her job, done properly, would answer it.
That was the moment the commission stopped being work and became something else, and she knew it at the time, and she wrote it down.

2 June. I have realised that the survey will answer the question whether I want it to or not. I am therefore going to do the survey properly and let it. I am recording here that I am aware of my own interest in the outcome, and that I intend to record everything I find whether or not it is convenient to me personally. If I fail to do that, this note is the evidence against me.
A swarm
There is one other thing from that fortnight and it belongs here rather than anywhere else.

On the twenty-eighth of May, at about eleven in the morning, Emrys Pike's fourth stock swarmed, and Ilse — who was in the churchyard with a clipboard, working her way along the north wall — heard it before she saw it: a sound like a distant aeroplane that was in fact about nine thousand insects coming over the yew hedge at head height.
She did what anybody does, which is to stand extremely still.
The swarm went over her and settled in the lower branches of a damson tree at the corner of the churchyard, in a hanging brown mass the size and shape of a rugby ball, and hummed to itself.
Emrys arrived four minutes later with a skep, a sheet and a pair of secateurs, walking, not running, because you do not run.
"You'll want to stand back."
"I'd rather stand here, if it's safe."

"It's safe. A swarm's got no house to defend and a bellyful of honey; it's the mildest thing in the world." He spread the sheet under the branch. "It's the only time in the year they'd let you do this to them."

She watched him take a swarm. It is one of the four or five most extraordinary things she ever saw. He cut the branch, and lowered the whole hanging mass into the skep in one motion, and set the skep upside down on the sheet with a stone under one edge, and stood back, and within ninety seconds the bees that were still in the air were walking up the sheet and in under the rim in a wide dark stream, thousands of them, in a hurry, going in.
"How do they know?"

"The queen's in there. They can smell her and they can hear the ones by the door telling them." He wiped his hands. "That's all a colony is, that. A great many small things agreeing about where the middle is."

Ilse wrote that down that evening in the back of her notebook, in the section she kept for things people said. She could not have explained then why it belonged with the log book and the fee book and a certified copy of a birth certificate issued at Ferrisport in 1949.
"Mr. Pike," she said. "May I ask you a dull question about your own family?"
The change in him was very small and very fast, and she saw it because she had been watching him take a swarm and was therefore watching him closely.
"I'm not a family man."
"No, I mean historically. For the record. There's a Pike child buried under the yew in 1942 with initials on the stone and no name. If it's a relation I'd want to record the relationship correctly."
He picked up the skep. He was careful with it; you are, with nine thousand of anything.
"That's my brother," said Emrys Pike, and walked away down the lane.
Ilse stood in the churchyard with a clipboard.

She had been an archivist for fourteen years and she knew exactly one thing about that answer, which was that a man who has a brother buried under a yew says my brother, and a man who does not have a brother buried under a yew says that's my brother, in the way you say the name of a thing you have practised saying.

She went back to the north wall and recorded eleven more stones before the light went, and her handwriting on that page is noticeably worse than on the pages either side of it, which is the sort of thing she would have noticed in somebody else's records at once.
The fee book
The burial fee book is a small red ledger, 1871 to date, and it records what was paid, by whom, for what, at every burial in the parish for a hundred years.

It is the least glamorous document in any parish chest and it is very frequently the most useful, because a register records what happened and a fee book records what somebody paid for, and money is much harder to falsify than sentiment.
Ilse opened it on the evening of the second of June and turned to February 1942 and found this:
14 Feb. Rhys (child). Grave, 12s 6d. Paid by parish.
14 Feb. Pike (child). Grave, 12s 6d. Paid, R. Pike.
17 Feb. Callow (child). Grave, 12s 6d. Paid, J. Callow.
21 Feb. Braith (2 children). Nil.
21 Feb. Braith. Nil.
Nil.

Not paid by parish, which is what is written when a family cannot pay and the parish stands the cost, as it had done nine days earlier for the Rhys child. Not a dash, which is what the same rector wrote in 1938 when the entry did not apply.
Nil, twice, in a book about money, in a hand that had written twelve shillings and sixpence three times that same fortnight.

Ilse Vanterpool sat back in a caravan in a doomed valley and understood, with the absolute clarity of a person who has spent fourteen years reading other people's accounts, that no grave had been dug on the twenty-first of February 1942, because nobody had paid the sexton to dig one, because there had been nobody to put in it.
